title: Learn by Doing: Object-Oriented Programming
lead: The topic sat as a paper: its objective questions, then every past question on classes, inheritance and polymorphism, each with its model answer, and the method taught from nothing.
intro:
Part A is the objective questions on this topic. Part B is past questions only, and this is where the biggest single question lives: the 25 mark bank account question on inheritance and polymorphism, plus Vehicle and TemperatureCheck from 24/25.

Those questions are marked on structure, so learn the shape of a class and write it the same way every time.

lockin.big: "Private fields, a constructor that sets them, getters and setters, and a method that does the work. That is encapsulation, and it is worth marks before the logic is even read."
lockin.sub: Overriding replaces a superclass method, same signature, in a subclass. Overloading is same name, different parameters, in one class. super() calls the parent constructor and must come first.

methodFrames.teach:
A class is a blueprint; an object is one thing built from it with new. The exam's class questions always want the same four parts: private fields, a constructor, getters and setters, and a method that does the work.

public class Student {    private String name;    private double cgpa;    public Student(String name, double cgpa) {        this.name = name;        this.cgpa = cgpa;    }    public String getName() { return name; }    public void setCgpa(double cgpa) {        if (cgpa >= 0 && cgpa <= 5) this.cgpa = cgpa;    }    public String classify() {        if (cgpa >= 4.5) return "First Class";        if (cgpa >= 3.5) return "Second Upper";        return "Lower";    }    public static void main(String[] args) {        Student s = new Student("Ada", 4.6);        System.out.println(s.getName() + ": " + s.classify());        s.setCgpa(9.9);        System.out.println("after a bad set: " + s.classify());    }}
OutputAda: First Class
after a bad set: First Class
methodFrames.ask: Read this and say what the constructor is for, and why the fields are private.

methodFrames.check: It sets the fields at creation; private fields force changes through a setter that can check them.
methodFrames.teach:
The constructor sets the fields when the object is created, and it has the class's name and no return type. The fields are private so nothing outside can set a CGPA of 9.9: the setter refused it, which is why the classification did not change.

That is encapsulation: data hidden behind methods that can validate it. Say the word AND the reason in the exam.
methodFrames.ask: What is this. for, in this.name = name?

methodFrames.check: It separates the field from the parameter of the same name.
methodFrames.teach:
this is the object the method was called on, so this.name is the FIELD and name alone is the PARAMETER. Without it the parameter would simply assign to itself and the field would stay empty.

class Vehicle {    protected int speed;    public Vehicle(int speed) { this.speed = speed; }    public void display() { System.out.println("Vehicle at " + speed); }}class Car extends Vehicle {    private int doors;    public Car(int speed, int doors) {        super(speed);        this.doors = doors;    }    @Override    public void display() { System.out.println("Car at " + speed + " with " + doors + " doors"); }}public class Ride {    public static void main(String[] args) {        Vehicle[] fleet = { new Vehicle(80), new Car(120, 4) };        for (Vehicle v : fleet) v.display();    }}
OutputVehicle at 80
Car at 120 with 4 doors
methodFrames.ask: Now inheritance. What does extends give the subclass, and what does super do?

methodFrames.check: extends inherits everything; super() calls the parent constructor first.
methodFrames.teach:
extends gives the subclass every field and method of the superclass, and super(speed) calls the parent constructor, which must be the first line of the child's constructor.

Now look at what the loop did: both objects are held in a Vehicle array, but each printed its OWN version of display.
methodFrames.ask: What is that called, and when does Java decide which display to run?

methodFrames.check: Polymorphism, decided at run time by the actual object.
methodFrames.teach:
Polymorphism, and the decision is made at RUN TIME, from the actual object rather than the declared type. That is dynamic method dispatch, and it is the sentence the 25 mark question is marked on.

The method in the child is an override: same name, same parameters, same return type. @Override is optional but it makes the compiler check you.
methodFrames.ask: Overriding against overloading, three differences. Say them before you read on.

methodFrames.check: Different parameters against identical ones, same class against subclass, compile time against run time.
methodFrames.teach:
Overloading: same name, DIFFERENT parameter lists, in the SAME class, resolved at COMPILE time. Overriding: same name and same parameters, in a SUBCLASS, resolved at RUN time. Overloading is about convenience; overriding is about replacing behaviour.

That is 25/26's three mark question, and it is three lines if you learn the pairs: where, what differs, when it is resolved.

scenario.text: [2 marks]A. Define encapsulation as an OOP principle

exam.problem: Write your answer to the question above in your book first. It carries 2 marks, so write one clear point for every mark. Then open the model answer and mark yourself against it.
exam.answer:
Q2 a · define encapsulation · 2 MARKS

Model answer.

Encapsulation is the OOP principle of bundling data (fields) and the methods that operate on them into a single unit (a class), while restricting direct access to some of its components.

In Java it is achieved by declaring the fields private and exposing controlled access through public getter and setter methods. This gives data hiding (unauthorised code cannot read or modify the state), validation (a setter can reject invalid input, for example preventing a negative balance), and flexibility (the internal representation can change without breaking any code that uses the class).

Where the marks are: one for the bundling-plus- restricting definition, one for how it is achieved (private fields, public getters and setters). Add one benefit if you have room. See Unit 6.4.

exam.answer:
Q2 b · three differences: overloading vs overriding · 3 MARKS

Model answer. Three differences, one mark each:

  1. Where they occur. Overloading happens within a single class: several methods share a name. Overriding happens between a superclass and a subclass: the subclass replaces the inherited method.
  2. The parameter list. Overloaded methods must have different parameter lists. An overriding method must have exactly the same name and parameter list as the one it overrides.
  3. When the method is chosen. Overloading is resolved at compile time by the compiler (static polymorphism); overriding is resolved at run time by the JVM, from the object's actual type (dynamic polymorphism).

Where the marks are: three separate axes. If you have room, add that overriding requires inheritance and overloading does not. See Unit 6.7.

questions.heading: 2025/2026, Question Four, 25 marks

scenario.text:
A bank wants a system representing different types of accounts using inheritance and polymorphism.

(9 marks)Part 1: Superclass BankAccount

i.    Create a class named BankAccount with private fields to hold the account number, the account holder's name, and the balance. Provide a constructor to initialise all three.

ii.   Create a method that adds a given amount to the balance.

iii.  Create a method that deducts a given amount from the balance if there are sufficient funds; otherwise, the transaction should be rejected and a message displayed.

iv.  Create a method that displays the account's current details: its account number, holder's name, and balance.

(10 marks)Part 2: Subclasses

i.    SavingAccount extends BankAccount. Override the withdrawal method so a withdrawal is only allowed if the balance after the withdrawal would still be >= ₦1,000. Otherwise, reject and display a message.

ii.   CurrentAccount extends BankAccount. Override the withdrawal method so that every successful withdrawal automatically adds a ₦50 reward to the balance afterward. (6 marks)

Part 3: Main Method

i.    Creates at least one SavingAccount and one CurrentAccount;

ii.   Deposits money into each;

iii.  Performs at least one successful and one unsuccessful/reward-triggering withdrawal on each;

iv.  Displays each account's details before and after the transactions;

v.   Demonstrates polymorphism by storing each object in a BankAccount reference and calling the withdrawal method through it, confirming that the correct overridden version runs.

The mark allocations are printed as shown: Part 1 is 9, Part 2 is 10, and a further "(6 marks)" is printed against Part 2 item ii. Part 3 carries no printed allocation. Reproduced as it appears.

exam.answer:
Q4 · inheritance and polymorphism · 25 MARKS

Part 1, BankAccount (9 marks). Private fields for account number, holder name and balance; a constructor initialising all three; a method that adds to the balance; a method that deducts if funds suffice and otherwise rejects with a message; a method that displays the details.

Part 2, subclasses (10 marks). SavingAccount overrides the withdrawal so it is allowed only if the balance after the withdrawal would still be >= 1000. CurrentAccount overrides it so every successful withdrawal adds a 50 reward afterwards.

Part 3, main (6 marks). One of each; deposit into each; at least one successful and one unsuccessful or reward-triggering withdrawal on each; details before and after; and demonstrate polymorphism by storing each object in a BankAccount reference and calling the withdrawal through it, confirming the correct overridden version runs.

Must memorise · The question contains a contradiction, and resolving it is the exam

Part 1 says the balance must be private.

Part 2 says the subclasses must change the balance.

A private field is invisible to a subclass. So the subclass cannot touch it.

This is not the examiner being careless. It is the whole of Units 6.4 and 6.6 arriving in one question: encapsulation says the field is private, and inheritance says the child must still be able to work with it. The way out is the only way out, and it is the answer being marked: the subclass goes through the parent's public methods, using getBalance() to read and super.withdraw(amount) or deposit(amount) to change.

MEMORY HOOK: the child knocks, it does not climb in through the window. getBalance() to look, super.withdraw() to act.

Trap · A subclass cannot see a private field, and it will say so

The tempting move is to write the arithmetic straight into the subclass. Java stops you at the compiler:

class Account {    private double balance = 5000;}class Saving extends Account {    public boolean withdraw(double amount) {        balance = balance - amount;        return true;    }}public class SubclassReach {    public static void main(String[] args) {        new Saving().withdraw(100);    }}
Compiler outputerror: balance has private access in Account

Private means the declaring class only, and a subclass is a different class. Inheritance gives Saving the field (every Saving object really does contain a balance) but not access to it. The field is there and untouchable, which is exactly what private is for (Unit 6.4).

Would protected fix it? It would compile, and it is the wrong answer here, because part 1 said private. Marks are for doing what the question said. Beyond the exam, going through the parent's methods is better anyway: every rule the parent enforces on a withdrawal keeps being enforced. Make the field protected and each subclass has to remember those rules for itself, which is how a bank ends up with an account that can be overdrawn down one code path and not another. See the access table in Unit 6.6.

Teach · Why withdraw returns boolean

The paper does not say what withdraw returns, and the obvious choice is void. Then read part 2 ii again: a CurrentAccount adds the reward on every successful withdrawal. Not on every attempt. So the override has to know whether the withdrawal succeeded, and a void method tells it nothing.

Making withdraw return boolean makes the override three honest lines:

boolean succeeded = super.withdraw(amount);if (succeeded) { deposit(50); }return succeeded;

The alternative, comparing the balance before and after, works but is worse: it re-derives an answer the parent already knew and threw away. When a method knows something the caller needs, it should return it. Notice that this decision is forced by a single word in part 2 ii, which is what "read the question" means in practice.

Code · question four, complete · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
// ===== Part 1: the superclass =====class BankAccount {    private String accountNumber;    private String holderName;    private double balance;    // Part 1 i: a constructor that initialises all three fields.    public BankAccount(String accountNumber, String holderName, double balance) {        this.accountNumber = accountNumber;        this.holderName = holderName;        this.balance = balance;    }    // The private fields are reachable only through these doors (Unit 6.4).    public String getAccountNumber() { return accountNumber; }    public String getHolderName()    { return holderName; }    public double getBalance()       { return balance; }    // Part 1 ii: add a given amount to the balance.    public void deposit(double amount) {        balance = balance + amount;        System.out.println("Deposit " + amount + " -> " + accountNumber            + " balance is now " + balance);    }    // Part 1 iii: deduct if funds are sufficient, otherwise reject with a message.    // Returns whether it succeeded, which is what CurrentAccount needs to know.    public boolean withdraw(double amount) {        if (amount <= balance) {            balance = balance - amount;            System.out.println("Withdraw " + amount + " -> " + accountNumber                + " balance is now " + balance);            return true;        }        System.out.println("REJECTED: " + accountNumber + " holds only " + balance            + ", so " + amount + " cannot be withdrawn");        return false;    }    // Part 1 iv: display the account's current details.    public void displayDetails() {        System.out.println("Account " + accountNumber + " | " + holderName            + " | balance " + balance);    }}// ===== Part 2 i: a saving account must never drop below 1000 =====class SavingAccount extends BankAccount {    public SavingAccount(String accountNumber, String holderName, double balance) {        super(accountNumber, holderName, balance);    }    @Override    public boolean withdraw(double amount) {        if (getBalance() - amount < 1000) {            System.out.println("REJECTED: a saving account must retain 1000. " +                "Withdrawing "                + amount + " from " + getAccountNumber() + " would leave "                + (getBalance() - amount));            return false;        }        return super.withdraw(amount);    }}// ===== Part 2 ii: every successful withdrawal earns a 50 reward =====class CurrentAccount extends BankAccount {    public CurrentAccount(String accountNumber, String holderName, double balance) {        super(accountNumber, holderName, balance);    }    @Override    public boolean withdraw(double amount) {        boolean succeeded = super.withdraw(amount);        if (succeeded) {            System.out.println("Reward earned on " + getAccountNumber() + ":");            deposit(50);        }        return succeeded;    }}// ===== Part 3: the main method =====public class BankSystem {    public static void main(String[] args) {        // Part 3 i: at least one of each.        SavingAccount saving   = new SavingAccount("SA-1001", "Ada Bello", 5000.0);        CurrentAccount current = new CurrentAccount("CA-2002", "Femi Okonkwo",            3000.0);        System.out.println("=== iv: details BEFORE the transactions ===");        saving.displayDetails();        current.displayDetails();        // Part 3 ii: deposit into each.        System.out.println("=== ii: deposit into each ===");        saving.deposit(2000.0);        current.deposit(1000.0);        // Part 3 iii: a successful and an unsuccessful withdrawal on each.        System.out.println("=== iii: a successful and an unsuccessful withdrawal on " +            "each ===");        saving.withdraw(4000.0);        saving.withdraw(2500.0);        current.withdraw(1000.0);        current.withdraw(999999.0);        System.out.println("=== iv: details AFTER the transactions ===");        saving.displayDetails();        current.displayDetails();        // Part 3 v: polymorphism. Same reference type, same call, same amount.        System.out.println("=== v: polymorphism, same reference type, same call, " +            "same amount ===");        BankAccount acc = new SavingAccount("SA-3003", "Ngozi Eze", 1500.0);        acc.withdraw(600.0);        acc.displayDetails();        acc = new CurrentAccount("CA-4004", "Tunde Ade", 1500.0);        acc.withdraw(600.0);        acc.displayDetails();    }}
Output=== iv: details BEFORE the transactions ===
Account SA-1001 | Ada Bello | balance 5000.0
Account CA-2002 | Femi Okonkwo | balance 3000.0
=== ii: deposit into each ===
Deposit 2000.0 -> SA-1001 balance is now 7000.0
Deposit 1000.0 -> CA-2002 balance is now 4000.0
=== iii: a successful and an unsuccessful withdrawal on each ===
Withdraw 4000.0 -> SA-1001 balance is now 3000.0
REJECTED: a saving account must retain 1000. Withdrawing 2500.0 from SA-1001 would leave 500.0
Withdraw 1000.0 -> CA-2002 balance is now 3000.0
Reward earned on CA-2002:
Deposit 50.0 -> CA-2002 balance is now 3050.0
REJECTED: CA-2002 holds only 3050.0, so 999999.0 cannot be withdrawn
=== iv: details AFTER the transactions ===
Account SA-1001 | Ada Bello | balance 3000.0
Account CA-2002 | Femi Okonkwo | balance 3050.0
=== v: polymorphism, same reference type, same call, same amount ===
REJECTED: a saving account must retain 1000. Withdrawing 600.0 from SA-3003 would leave 900.0
Account SA-3003 | Ngozi Eze | balance 1500.0
Withdraw 600.0 -> CA-4004 balance is now 900.0
Reward earned on CA-4004:
Deposit 50.0 -> CA-4004 balance is now 950.0
Account CA-4004 | Tunde Ade | balance 950.0

All four classes live in one file because only one may be public and that one must match the file name: BankSystem.java. In the hall, write them as four classes exactly as they are here, or as four separate files. Both are correct.

Dry run · Every balance, and why each rule fired
Callbalance beforewhich rule decidedallowed?balance after
SA-1001, a SavingAccount, opens at 5000
deposit(2000)5000.0no rule: deposits always landyes7000.0
withdraw(4000)7000.07000 - 4000 = 3000, and 3000 >= 1000yes3000.0
withdraw(2500)3000.03000 - 2500 = 500, and 500 < 1000no3000.0
CA-2002, a CurrentAccount, opens at 3000
deposit(1000)3000.0no ruleyes4000.0
withdraw(1000)4000.0funds suffice, so the reward firesyes3000.0, then +50 = 3050.0
withdraw(999999)3050.0funds do not suffice, so no rewardno3050.0

The last row is the one to study. The reward sits inside if (succeeded), so a rejected withdrawal earns nothing. Had withdraw returned void, that if could not have been written, and CA-2002 would have been paid 50 for a transaction that never happened.

Must memorise · How to prove polymorphism in six lines

Part 3 v asks you to confirm the correct overridden version runs. A proof needs a control: change one thing and show the behaviour changes.

So: same reference type, same method, same amount, same starting balance. Only the object differs.

BankAccount acc = new SavingAccount("SA-3003", "Ngozi Eze", 1500.0);acc.withdraw(600.0);        // rejected: would leave 900, under 1000acc = new CurrentAccount("CA-4004", "Tunde Ade", 1500.0);acc.withdraw(600.0);        // allowed, and pays a 50 reward: 950

Both variables are declared BankAccount. Both calls are acc.withdraw(600.0), character for character. Both accounts hold 1500.0. One is refused and one is paid a bonus.

That is the proof, and here is the sentence that earns the mark: the compiler only knew acc was a BankAccount, so the choice of which withdraw to run could not have been made at compile time. It was made at run time, from the object's actual class. That is dynamic method dispatch, and it is what "polymorphism" names (Unit 6.7).

MEMORY HOOK: the reference decides what you may call. The object decides what actually runs.

Compare this with the TRAP at the end of Unit 6.6, where the same setup silently ran the parent's method because the override was really an overload. Same two lines of code, opposite outcomes, and the difference was one parameter type. That is why @Override sits on every override here.

questions.heading: 2024/2025, Question Four, 7.5 marks

scenario.text:
[7.5 marks]D. Write a program to define a class called TemperatureCheck with the following specifications:

i.    Data field (state): double temperature.

ii.   A constructor method to set the temperature

iii.  A method called evaluateTemperature() that uses if-else statements to output:

a.  "Too Cold" if temperature < 15

b.  "Normal" if the temperature is between 15 and 30 (inclusive)

c.  "Too Hot" if temperature > 30.

iv.  In your main method, prompt the user to enter a temperature value, create an object of the class, and display the evaluation result. Use JOptionPane to accept inputs.

Watch"between 15 and 30 (inclusive)" means >= 15 && <= 30, and the boundary values 15 and 30 are exactly where a marker checks. The paper also insists on if-else, so a switch does not answer it.

exam.answer:
Q4 d · the temperaturecheck class · 7.5 MARKS
Must memorise · "Between 15 and 30 inclusive" needs no upper test

if (t < 15) "Too Cold";
else if (t <= 30) "Normal";
else "Too Hot";

The else if only runs when t < 15 was false, which already means t >= 15. So writing else if (t >= 15 && t <= 30) is not wrong, it is redundant: the ladder has already established the lower bound. Let the structure carry what it has proved (Unit 4.2).

The two boundaries are the marks. "Inclusive" means 15 and 30 are both Normal. Get < and <= the wrong way round and the program is right for 99% of inputs and wrong on exactly the two values the examiner will test.

MEMORY HOOK: test the fences, not the field. When a spec names a boundary, that boundary is the test case.

Code · q4 d, complete · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
import java.util.Scanner;// i. the class, with its one data fieldclass TemperatureCheck {    private double temperature;    // ii. a constructor that sets the temperature    public TemperatureCheck(double temperature) {        this.temperature = temperature;    }    // iii. if-else evaluation    public void evaluateTemperature() {        if (temperature < 15) {            System.out.println("Too Cold");        } else if (temperature <= 30) {            System.out.println("Normal");        } else {            System.out.println("Too Hot");        }    }}public class TemperatureDemo {    public static void main(String[] args) {        Scanner in = new Scanner(System.in);        while (in.hasNextLine()) {            String line = in.nextLine();            if (line.isEmpty()) continue;            double t = Double.parseDouble(line);            System.out.print(t + " -> ");            TemperatureCheck check = new TemperatureCheck(t);            check.evaluateTemperature();        }    }}
Output5.0 -> Too Cold
15.0 -> Normal
22.0 -> Normal
30.0 -> Normal
31.0 -> Too Hot
40.0 -> Too Hot

Read rows 2 and 4: 15.0 and 30.0 are both Normal, which is exactly what "inclusive" demands, and 31.0 is the first Too Hot. The values were chosen to sit on the fences. In the hall this reads double t = Double.parseDouble(JOptionPane.showInputDialog("Enter a temperature:")); and the result goes out through showMessageDialog (F.11); the loop here exists only so one run can show you all six cases.

The field is private and set only by the constructor, which is Unit 6.4's encapsulation arriving without being asked for. The question says "data field (state)"; making it private costs one word and is never wrong.

exam.answer:
Q5 a · describe inheritance, polymorphism and method overriding · 3 MARKS

Model answer.

  1. Inheritance. One class acquiring the fields and methods of another with extends, so the subclass has everything the superclass has without repeating it, and may add or replace behaviour. It models an is-a relationship: a Bicycle is a Vehicle.
  2. Polymorphism. One reference, many behaviours: a variable of the superclass type may hold an object of any subclass, and a call through it runs the object's own version, decided at run time. "Many forms".
  3. Method overriding. A subclass supplying its own version of a method the superclass already has, with the same signature, which replaces the inherited one for objects of that subclass.

Where the marks are: these three are one idea in three parts, and saying so earns the mark. Inheritance makes the family; overriding makes the members differ; polymorphism is what you get when you then hold any of them in one variable and call the method. Distinguish overriding (same signature, subclass, run time) from overloading (different parameters, same class, compile time), which is Q1 of this same paper. Units 6.6 and 6.7.

Compiler outputerror: not a statement

The errors, listed.

  1. int nums = {10, 20, 30}; is not an array. A list in braces needs an array type. Fix: int[] nums = {10, 20, 30};
  2. nums[3] does not exist. Three elements means indexes 0, 1 and 2. And the label says "Middle value", so the intent is nums[1], which is 20. Say both halves: the index is out of bounds and the middle of three is index 1.
  3. i <= nums.length is off by one and would throw at nums[3]. Fix: i < nums.length.
  4. i never increments. Fix: i++.
  5. "Sum is: " + ); has nothing to add. Fix: "Sum is: " + sum.

The output after correction:

OutputMiddle value is: 20
Sum is: 60
Code · q5 c corrected · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
public class MiddleValue {    public static void main(String[] args) {        int[] nums = {10, 20, 30};        System.out.println("Middle value is: " + nums[1]);        int sum = 0;        for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {            sum += nums[i];        }        System.out.println("Sum is: " + sum);    }}
OutputMiddle value is: 20
Sum is: 60

Errors 3 and 4 are the same two errors as Q2 B on this paper, character for character. The off-by-one and the missing increment are this examiner's signature. They are on both papers, in both years. Learn them once.

questions.heading: 2024/2025, Question Five, 7.5 marks

scenario.text:
[7.5 marks]D. Write a program using inheritance and method overriding as follows:

i.    Create a superclass called Vehicle with the following:

a.  An instance variable speed (int)

b.  A constructor that initialises speed

c.  A method displayInfo() that prints "Vehicle speed: <speed> km/h"

ii.   Create a subclass called Bicycle that overrides the displayInfo() method to print: "Bicycle speed: <speed> km/h. This is an eco-friendly ride."

iii.  In the main method:

a.  Create an object of class Vehicle with a speed of 80

b.  Create an object of class Bicycle with a speed of 25

c.  Call displayInfo() on both objects to demonstrate polymorphism.

questions.asked:
Shape: Write a program. A full program, marked on structure as much as on logic. The two papers set this shape 17 times between them, 3 of them on this topic.

And the subject repeats: a program built on inheritance and polymorphism is also set in 2025/2026, Question Four, 25 marks.

breakdown.question: What is this question actually asking, what have you been given, and what do the marks tell you about how much to write? Decide, then check.
breakdown.answer:
GivenA full specification, including the exact strings to print.
Asked forTwo classes and a main that proves polymorphism.
The marks7.5 marks. The printed strings are quoted in the paper, so reproduce them exactly, km/h and full stop included.
Watch<speed> is a placeholder for the value, not text to print. And to "demonstrate polymorphism" the objects should be held in Vehicle references, or you have demonstrated nothing.
Taught inUnits 8.1 to 8.6.

exam.answer:
Q5 d · vehicle and bicycle · 7.5 MARKS
Code · q5 d, complete · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
// i. the superclassclass Vehicle {    protected int speed;    public Vehicle(int speed) {        this.speed = speed;    }    public void displayInfo() {        System.out.println("Vehicle speed: " + speed + " km/h");    }}// ii. the subclass, overriding displayInfo()class Bicycle extends Vehicle {    public Bicycle(int speed) {        super(speed);    }    @Override    public void displayInfo() {        System.out.println("Bicycle speed: " + speed            + " km/h. This is an eco-friendly ride.");    }}public class VehicleDemo {    public static void main(String[] args) {        // iii a/b. one of each        Vehicle car = new Vehicle(80);        Bicycle bike = new Bicycle(25);        // iii c. call displayInfo() on both        car.displayInfo();        bike.displayInfo();        // and the polymorphic form the question is really after        Vehicle[] fleet = {new Vehicle(80), new Bicycle(25)};        System.out.println("-- through a Vehicle reference --");        for (Vehicle v : fleet) {            v.displayInfo();        }    }}
OutputVehicle speed: 80 km/h
Bicycle speed: 25 km/h. This is an eco-friendly ride.
-- through a Vehicle reference --
Vehicle speed: 80 km/h
Bicycle speed: 25 km/h. This is an eco-friendly ride.
Teach · The last four words of the question change the answer

The question says: call displayInfo() on both objects to demonstrate polymorphism. Read literally, parts a to c are satisfied by:

Vehicle car = new Vehicle(80);Bicycle bike = new Bicycle(25);car.displayInfo();bike.displayInfo();

That prints the two required lines, and it demonstrates nothing. Each variable's declared type already matches its object exactly, so the compiler could have picked both methods without any run-time decision. Overriding happened, but polymorphism was never tested.

Polymorphism needs the reference to be the SUPERCLASS type, so that the declared type and the actual object disagree and only the run time can settle it:

Vehicle[] fleet = {new Vehicle(80), new Bicycle(25)};
for (Vehicle v : fleet) v.displayInfo();

Now every element is declared Vehicle, the loop body is one identical call, and it still prints two different lines. That is the demonstration, and it is what the last four words are asking for. The listing above does both: the literal answer first, then the proof.

Same idea as Q4 part 3 v on the 2025/26 paper, where the reference is explicitly required to be a BankAccount. Two papers, two years, one point: the reference decides what you may call, the object decides what runs.
